messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: I understand the worry about crime, but I think forcing local police into federal immigration enforcement actually makes communities less safe. When officers are seen as an arm of federal agents, people stop calling them for help. Victims and witnesses who fear a relative could be deported often choose silence over cooperation, and that silence lets real danger go unaddressed. Local police exist to handle local law, not to carry out a separate federal mission with different goals and different rules.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I understand that trust matters, and I won't deny that fear can silence people. But in my view the greater risk comes from releasing someone accused of a serious crime simply because a city chose not to notify federal authorities. Public safety shouldn't hinge on immigration status once someone is booked for a dangerous offense. If a jail ignores a federal flag on a person in custody, that isn't about protecting witnesses, it's about letting a specific concern go unanswered. I think cooperation should be the default, not the exception, especially for serious offenders.

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: That's a fair concern, and I agree public safety matters enormously. But I think there's a meaningful difference between shielding witnesses and victims, which limited-cooperation policies are designed to do, and pretending that all cooperation automatically makes neighborhoods safer. Blanket cooperation policies often sweep up people never convicted of anything, based only on suspicion, and that erodes trust broadly, not just for the accused. I'd rather cities set narrow, clear rules for genuinely dangerous cases than have police departments function as default extensions of federal enforcement for everyone.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I think that distinction is worth considering, but drawing the line at limiting cooperation puts police in the position of second-guessing federal requests instead of simply supporting law enforcement across levels of government. Once someone is arrested, I don't think local officers should be shielded from working with federal counterparts just because a city prefers otherwise. If someone is dangerous, all levels of government should be able to communicate freely without artificial barriers. Regardless of where an accusation originates, anyone arrested still faces the same local courts and the same criminal charges as any other resident. [[CLAIM]]
